items.title: How much does a shared table move the risk needle, compared to call traffic?
items.description: Using the unit's own e-commerce example, drag how many database tables a candidate group still shares with modules staying behind. Cross-module calls per day are held fixed at the Orders/Shipping baseline (3,000/day) — the point is watching how much faster risk climbs from shared tables alone than it ever does from call volume. A score under 20 reads as a clean boundary; over 50 is the same shape as the Orders-alone mistake from L1's scenario.

params.name: sharedTables
params.label: Tables still shared with modules outside the group

items.compute: const splitRiskScore = Math.min(100, Math.round(params.sharedTables * 9 + params.callsPerDayThousands * 1.2)); return { splitRiskScore };

items.title: Does adding more modules to a candidate group always look better?
items.description: Start from the Shipping+Fulfillment pair (internal call ratio ~76% per L2) and drag how many extra, loosely-related modules get bundled in alongside them for the sole purpose of inflating the ratio. Each added module contributes a little internal traffic but a lot more external traffic of its own, since it wasn't actually chosen for cohesion — watch how the ratio climbs from bundling size rather than genuine cohesion, exactly the gaming risk L2 warned about.
items.compute: const baseInternal = 76; const baseExternal = 24; const addedInternalPerModule = 4; const addedExternalPerModule = 9; const internal = baseInternal + params.extraModulesBundled * addedInternalPerModule; const external = baseExternal + params.extraModulesBundled * addedExternalPerModule; const internalCallRatioPercent = Math.round((internal / (internal + external)) * 100); return { internalCallRatioPercent };

items.title: How does an ambiguous class's table access split affect classification confidence?
items.description: Reproduces the unit's own ShippingLabel example: it accesses 40 shipping_labels rows against a varying number of order_items rows. Drag order_items access up from the baseline (5) and watch suggestBoundary's confidence in "Shipping" fall as the split gets less lopsided — caller counts are held fixed at the unit's numbers (30 Shipping callers, 2 Orders callers).
items.compute: const shippingLabelsAccess = 40; const shippingCallers = 30; const ordersCallers = 2; const shippingScore = shippingLabelsAccess + shippingCallers * 0.5; const ordersScore = params.orderItemsAccess + ordersCallers * 0.5; const total = shippingScore + ordersScore; const confidencePercent = Math.round((shippingScore / total) * 100); return { confidencePercent };
